I've been a gastroenterologist for 18 years.

And the single most overlooked complaint I see in women on GLP-1 medications is upstream stomach slowdown.

They haven't gone in four days. Their stomach feels like cement, and every burp brings the taste of rotten eggs. They've tried Miralax, magnesium, fiber gummies, stool softeners, Smooth Move tea, prunes — sometimes $400 worth of products in a single month, none of them working consistently and none of them actually fixing what's underneath.

And every time they go to their doctor, the answer is the same: "Drink more water. Take more fiber."

But here's what I've been telling my patients — and what most general practitioners aren't trained to consider:

Your constipation isn't a colon problem.

It's a stomach problem.

Ozempic®, Wegovy®, Mounjaro®, and Zepbound® work by slowing gastric emptying. That's part of how they reduce appetite. But for a lot of women, the stomach slows so much that food sits for hours longer than it should. It ferments. Gas builds. Sulfur burps appear. The bottleneck is six feet upstream from where every laxative on your nightstand is aimed.

Your colon isn't broken. Your stomach's just stopped moving.

That's why Miralax works inconsistently. Fiber makes you more bloated rather than less. Nothing in your medicine cabinet has actually fixed it — those products are aimed at the wrong organ.

I wrote a full breakdown of the 5 warning signs that your GLP-1 constipation is actually an upstream stomach problem — not a colon problem. If you've been struggling with this for weeks or months and can't figure out why nothing is working, this is worth 6 minutes of your time.
creative.title: 5 Warning Signs Your GLP-1 Constipation Is a Stomach Problem — Not a "Colon Problem"
